In 1932, a 27-year-old Polish mathematician broke Enigma with pencil and permutation theory.
Every message began with a three-letter key, typed twice. So letters one and four were always the same letter, scrambled two ways.
About eighty messages a day gave him chains, letter one to letter four, and the chains closed into loops.
One real day: loops of ten, ten, two, two, one and one.
The plugboard shuffled which letters sat in the loops, but it could never change their sizes.
That shape was a fingerprint of the rotor setting, whatever the cables did.
So the Poles catalogued every shape: 105,456 positions, one card each.
Then Zygalski's perforated sheets, stacked over a light, narrowed it to a single hole.
Shape beat scramble. So why did Britain still need Turing's Bombe?
This is LATOON. Voyaging the Unseen.
